data.title: Novohrad (Nógrád) – a Slavic hillfort that became a county seat (H)
data.excerpt: An isolated hill of volcanic origin above the village of Nógrád in Hungary, 286 m above sea level, carries the clearly visible ruins of a medieval castle. The Slavs found older ramparts here, renewed them and so built a “New Stronghold” – Novohrad, a hillfort of exceptional importance whose name survives in the Hungarian Nógrád and in the name of the county.
data.metaTitle: Novohrad (Nógrád) – the hillfort that named a county
data.metaDescription: On a volcanic hill above Nógrád the Slavs rebuilt older ramparts into a “New Stronghold” – Novohrad, which later gave its name to the whole county.

keyFacts.label: Origin of the name
keyFacts.value: the Slavic “New Stronghold” (Novigrad) — preserved to this day in the Hungarian name Nógrád and in the name of the Novohrad (Nógrád) county

keyFacts.label: The outer castle
keyFacts.value: irregular in shape, measuring approximately 140 × 90 m, protected by three large bastions of the Italian type filled with earth

keyFacts.label: The inner castle
keyFacts.value: separated from the outer one by a ditch 30 feet wide and equally deep, cut into the rock; it held a palace, a tower and a well hewn into the rock

keyFacts.label: Its fate in the Ottoman era
keyFacts.value: the castle fell into Turkish hands twice; in 1685 it was wrecked by an explosion of gunpowder after a lightning strike

children.text: Above the village of Nógrád (Hungary) rises an isolated hill of volcanic origin, resembling a huge loaf of bread, on which the ruins of a medieval castle are clearly visible. The elevation of the hill is 286 m, its relative height around 50 – 60 m, and the rounded slopes all around are very steep – in short, it is a very suitable place for controlling a wide area and can be defended superbly.

We do not know who first made use of the natural conditions here to build the earliest fortification; in the Migration Period the Slavs already found older primitive defensive ramparts here, which they renewed and improved, thereby in fact building a “New Stronghold”, and they gave it that name as well (the chronicle of Anonymus, for example, mentions it as “Castrum Nougrad”, and the foundation charter of the Buda chapter of 1299 calls it “Castrum Novigrad”).

blocks.alt: On a map of 1739 we still see the Slovak name Novigrad

children.text: Today we no longer know what the Slavic Novohrad – Novigrad looked like at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries; at that time massive rampart defences were being built with a timber box construction that was filled with earth. In any case, it was a hillfort of exceptional importance, an administrative centre headed by a župan, and it remained so after the arrival of the Hungarians as well, when it became a comital castle and the Novohrad county was named after it.

At first a royal castle, it changed owners from time to time, it also had to defend itself against raids by the Hussites, twice it fell into Turkish hands... and each time something on it had to be repaired or improved.

The Slavic ramparts, and any first stone buildings in the protected space behind them, were covered over or destroyed by numerous medieval additions and rebuildings, including earthworks on the crown of the castle hill.

children.text: The most important rebuilding was carried out in 1475 – 1506 by Bishop Mikuláš Báthori, when he had the so-called inner castle built to the plans of an Italian architect, separated from the outer castle by a ditch 30 feet wide and equally deep, cut into the rock. The outer castle, irregular in shape (measuring approximately 140 × 90 m), was protected by three large bastions of the Italian type, which were built on the slopes and, once completed, filled with earth, thereby gaining further space inside the protected precinct. Behind the high walls of the inner castle a palace and a tower were raised, and a well hewn into the rock was added as well. In 1685 lightning struck the tower where gunpowder was stored, and the ensuing explosion wrecked the inner castle so badly that the Turks were forced to abandon it.

No one ever repaired the ruins of the castle again; on the contrary — in 1709 they were demolished still more thoroughly, first by the Kuruc and then by the Labanc, simply so that the other side should gain no use from it.
